SUBJECT:  APPROVE REVISION TO THE HOUSING AUTHORITY OF THE CITY
  OF PALMDALE’S SELF-IMPOSED MAXIMUM SPACE RENT FOR
  INCOME-QUALIFYING SPACES FOR THE BOULDERS MOBILE
  HOME PARKS, ESTABLISH SPACE RENT SUBSIDY PROGRAM
  FOR BOULDERS MOBILE HOME PARKS AND AUTHORIZE THE
  AUTHORITY EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR OR HER DESIGNEE TO
  REVIEW AND APPROVE NON-SUBSTANTIAL REVISIONS FOR
  ANNUAL SPACE RENT INCREASES AND THE BOULDERS MOBILE
  HOME SPACE RENT SUBSIDY PROGRAM

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the Housing Authority:

  1. Approve the revision to the Housing Authority’s self-imposed maximum rent for
  income-qualifying spaces for the Boulders Mobile Home Parks;
  2. Establish a Space Rent Subsidy Program for the Boulders Mobile Home Parks;
  and,
  3. Authorize the Executive Director or her designee to review and approve non-
  substantial revisions for Boulders Mobile Home Parks space rent increases and
  the Boulders Mobile Home Parks Space Rent Subsidy Program.

BACKGROUND

In 1997, the Boulders Mobile Home Parks (Parks) were acquired by the Housing Authority
of the City of Palmdale (Housing Authority) to transfer to a nonprofit, Linc Housing. The
Housing Authority reacquired the Parks in 2002. The three Parks are Boulders at Ranch
I, with 358 spaces; boulders at Ranch II, with 206 spaces; and Boulders at the Lakes,
with 223 spaces, for a total of 787 spaces; these include 3 spaces for Manager units. In
2003, staff were encouraged to address the high space rents for the residents, which
were over $500 per month. The Housing Authority approved a maximum monthly space
rent of $360. On May 7, 2008, the Housing Authority approved a maximum space rent of

$400 per month for income-qualifying spaces. Annual monthly space rent increases were
at 2%, bringing many eligible residents to the maximum space rent by 2013, a five-year
period. The 1997 Bond Regulatory Agreement and Declaration of Restrictive Covenants
(Regulatory Agreement) does not restrict rents for non-qualifying and non-compliant
spaces and allows establishing space rent at an unrestricted “market” level. The current
space rent for non-qualifying units is $500 per month. Storage agreements for residents
storing items, including but not limited to recreational vehicles, old cars, and boats are not
restricted under the Regulatory Agreement.

DISCUSSION

In the past 15 years, since 2008, the operating costs for the three Parks have increased
annually, with a 21% increase from 2022 to 2023 and a 17% increase this current year.
In addition, maintenance of the facilities, including streets, retaining walls, and trees, is
required. Most of the 784 units have reached the maximum space rent of $400 and have
not received a rent increase since 2012. The current leases provide for an increase
“based on one-half (1/2) of the annual increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for the
Los Angeles, Anaheim, Riverside area, utilizing “All Urban Consumers” index as of the
latest available CPI for the month during which the notice of increase is given, or two
percent of the previous year’s base rent, whichever is greater.”

The August 2023 JLT Market Report for Los Angeles County surveyed 94 mobile home
park communities and reported an average adjusted monthly rent of $1,103 and an
average rent for all age properties under rent control ordinances is $887.

A market survey for the Antelope Valley conducted in June 2023 has monthly space rents
ranging from $450 to $920.

The February 26, 2024, Mobile Home Park Rental Review Board Staff Report provides
the space rents for new leases for the mobile home parks in Palmdale under the space
rent control ordinance ranging from $379 to $1,200, with the median rent of $700 and
average rent of $804.

The annual increase experienced by Palmdale mobile home parks under the rent control
ordinance from 2016-2024 has ranged from 1.09% to 4.93%. If the Parks’ residents had
not reached the approved maximum space rent, the space rent would have annually
averaged two (2) percent.

To continue to meet the Parks obligations and maintain the current level of service and
amenities, Staff recommends:

    Removing the maximum space rent;
    Increase space rent in accordance with the lease terms;

    For current leases, the increase to the monthly space rent will range from $8 to
  $9 for the first 10 years;
    Increase the space rent for new residents to $650 for qualifying spaces and $800
  for spaces whose residents choose not to provide the required annual certification;
    Leases for new residents will provide for an annual space rent increase of three
  percent per year or one-half (1/2) of CPI, whichever is greater;
    No changes are proposed for Storage Agreements: and,
    Staff will annually monitor market rate rents and the financial progress of the parks
  to determine if this policy requires adjustment.

Due to increase in basic living expenses, residents have expressed concern regarding
increasing rents, especially for retired residents on a fixed income. The Housing Authority
proposes a space rent assistance program for households experiencing challenges with
increased space rent. The subsidy would be limited to:

    The increase in space rent;
    Funded through the Parks operations budget;
    Residents must apply annually;
    The number of residents assisted is based on available funds; and,
    The criteria for the program are the most vulnerable residents who qualify as low-
  income based on the State of California Department of Housing and Community
  Development income limits, not qualified or receiving other assistance, and with
  housing costs equaling over 50% of their monthly income.

The comments received at the March 20, 2024 Council meeting have been addressed as
follows:

Boulders at the Lakes
   Cypress trees were checked by Tip Top Arborists who reported the trees are in
  good health, gypsy moths were not found and advised insects such as caterpillars
  can be controlled with the application of a systemic, such as BioAdvanced for
  Trees and Shrubs. The systemic will be applied as necessary;
   Service on the sewer lines will be increased to biannually from annually;
   Christmas lights on the spaces were verified to have been removed by March 16,
  2024, or they did not have lights with one space receiving a follow-up inspection;
   Visitor Parking signs are being removed as the spaces have been used for guest
  and resident vehicles;
   Parking on the street is being monitored and the concerns provided have been
  followed up;
   Playground equipment is monitored monthly for safety and has passed inspection;
   Additional lighting is being added as requested.
 Report to Chair and Commissioners of the Housing Authority

Safety Concerns
   A resident expressed concerns regarding safety in the event of an evacuation. In
  2023, the City coordinated CERT training for residents of all three Boulders Mobile
  Home Parks and their managers.
   The Emergency Preparedness Program is available at all three of the Park Offices;
   One Call Now system is in place at the Lakes to communicate with residents in the
  event of an emergency.

Other
   Spaces have annual inspections in early Spring and extra dumpsters are provided
  to assist the residents in addressing their Spring cleaning.
   Resident mailboxes are being replaced at Boulders at Ranch I and II.

These and other actions are taken to maintain the three Boulders Mobile Home Parks as
a great place to call home and are funded through the annual operations budgets.

FISCAL IMPACT

$72,768 revenue and $10,000 expense; Increased revenue and expenditures will take
effect in Fiscal Year 2024-25 and will be proposed in the annual operating budget.
Sufficient funds are in Boulders at the Ranch I reserve for the estimated cost of the slurry
seal of streets of $100,000 and will be proposed in the 2024-25 budget. CDBG funds
are requested in the 2024-25 Action Plan for ADA Improvements of one playground.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the Housing Authority:

  1. Adopt Resolution HA 2024-003, a resolution of the Housing Authority of the City of
  Palmdale, approving an amendment of Agreement No. 07-IIG-4212 (A-8212) with
  the State of California Department of Housing and Community Development for
  the Proposition 1-C Infill Infrastructure Grant Program; and,

  2. Authorize the Executive Director or her designee to execute amendments and
  documents related to the Proposition 1-C Infill Infrastructure Grant Program
  Agreement with the State of California Department of Housing and Community
  Development, including, without limitation, the requested amendment.

BACKGROUND

The Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale and Community
Development Associates, Inc. entered into Agreement No. 07-IIG-4212 (A-8212) with the
State of California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) on
October 24, 2011, for the Proposition 1-C Infill Infrastructure Grant (IIG) Program. The
funding received for the Proposition 1-C Infill and Infrastructure Grant Program was used
for development of the infrastructure necessary for construction of the For sale
Townhome Project and the Wright Brothers Court Apartment Project, located at 4th Street
East and East Avenue Q.

The Agreement was amended on October 2, 2012, replacing the Community
Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale with the Housing Authority of the City of

Palmdale. The Agreement was next amended on February 23, 2023 with the following
changes:

    STD 213A, Item 1 deleting Community Development Associates;
    STD Item 2, the Agreement term was changed to be 10/24/2011 through
  12/31/2026;
    Exhibit A Performance Milestone Housing Schedule was updated extending the
  milestones through December 31, 2026;
    Exhibit B, Section 4 Completion Dates were revised; and,
    The Entire Exhibit E, Special Terms and Conditions were replaced.

DISCUSSION

The 2011 Agreement, as amended, requires the development of 46 affordable for sale
townhomes on property owned by the Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale, as
successor housing agency, (Housing Authority). The Housing Authority requested a
Feasibility Study by Keyser Marston Associates of the cost of developing the affordable
for-sale townhomes versus the proceeds that would be received from the sale of the
townhomes and the subsidy required to meet the affordability requirement. The estimated
financial gap of development of 46 affordable for-sale townhome units required $15
million more than would be received in sales revenue for the townhome units.

Based on the Feasibility Study, the Housing Authority is requesting from HCD an
amendment of the Agreement amending Exhibit A Section 2, the chart of housing to be
developed and restricted on the Housing Authority property. The requested amendment
would change the required housing from affordable for sale townhomes at 80% and 120%
Income Limits (% of AMI) to affordable rental units at 60% Income Limits (% of AMI).

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; There is no fiscal impact associated with this action.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council receive and file the monthly investment activity

BACKGROUND

Pursuant to Section 16 of the City and Successor Agency Investment Policy, the City
Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on investments to
the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The reports shall
detail the type of investment, issuer’s name , purchase date, date of maturity, amount
of deposit, and interest rate. This information shall be provided for all City and Successor
Agency pooled investments, as well as for Certificates of Participation, Revenue Bonds,
Tax Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts, and Community Facilities District accounts,
which are managed by outside Fiscal Agents.

The monthly investment reports provide a synopsis of the investment activity for the City
and Successor Agency. The reports provide information on assets, allocations, average
maturities, yields, and book valuations. The interest rates presented are the most current
rates available as of the date of this report.

The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable sources of market prices.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entities’ investment policies 1)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations; 2) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient
liquidity to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash
requirements; and 3) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive
market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on is providing liquidity to measure
up to the City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the Finance
Division invests in two pooled funds, Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) and
California Asset Management Program (CAMP). These are intended for daily
operational activities and used for economic uncertainties and maintenance needs.
The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the City and Successor
Agency meet cash flow requirements.

The total LAIF balance for the City at the end of February is $120,013,401, a decrease
of $10,000,000 from the prior month due to a transfer to the general fund to meet
operating expenditures.

Successor Agency LAIF balance at the end of February was $6,283,347. No changes
were reported from the prior month.

CAMP’s balance for the City at the end of February was $20,372,951 compared to the
January balance of $15,288,256. The increase is due to a transfer made to CAMP
from General bank, and interest earned during the month.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve the Third Agreement to Professional Services Agreement A-7459 with
  Lance, Soll, & Lunghard, LLP for an additional amount of $110,000, for a total not
  to exceed amount of $347,400 for the remainder of the term through March 30,

BACKGROUND

On August 1, 2021, the City entered into an agreement with Lance, Soll, & Lunghard
LLP, a Certified Public Accounting (CPA) firm, to provide implementation and ongoing
support of CaseWare, a software that streamlines the production of the City’s Annual
Comprehensive Financial Reports (ACFR). CaseWare was fully implemented in Fiscal
Year 2021-22. With the ongoing support and use of customized templates within the
software, the City has been able to automate processes that have resulted in a reduction
in staff time and manual processes, standardized statement presentation, and reduced
risk of error in statements. These automations have positively impacted the annual
financial audit by decreasing the timeline for completion.

The third amendment to the agreement is being requested to provide ongoing
professional service support hours to assist in the completion of the City’s Annual
Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR), as well as the component unit reports for the
Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale, the Palmdale Civic Authority, the Palmdale
Financing Authority, and the Palmdale Community Foundation for FY 2024-25 and FY
2025-26. Support hours are billed as incurred; therefore, the City will only be charged for
used hours of service.

Lance, Soll & Lunghard, LLP is the largest accounting firm in Orange County, California,
and has been in business for 95 years. Their knowledge and expertise will continue to
benefit the City, solidifying our financial strength and positioning us for future growth and
stability. They have extensive experience in financial reporting, getting the most out of
CaseWare, automating accounting processes, and providing support and training to
California cities, counties, school districts, and other special districts.

  A. PURPOSE
  1. To establish uniform guidelines for naming and renaming City assets to best
  serve the City’s interests and to ensure a worthy and enduring legacy. This
  policy outlines the criteria, conditions, and procedures that govern the
  naming and renaming process to maintain their integrity and recognize
  outstanding community giving while acknowledging public investments.
  B. POLICY
  1. The City will adopt a name for City assets based on one or more of the following
  criteria:
  i. Location. As a general policy, a name should assist the public in identifying
  its location. The City shall first consider the name of the nearby
  neighborhood, landmark, geographical identification, natural or
  topographical features, and adjacent schools and streets; or
  ii. Historical Significance. Names that have recognizable historical
  significance associated with Palmdale. Examples include the history of a
  major event, place, or person that plays a vital role in preserving and
  honoring a community’s history; or
  iii. Outstanding Individuals. This category is designed to honor those who have
  served the City in an exceptional and distinguished manner, and as such,
  an asset of commensurate value may be selected. Recognition is
  acceptable should their contribution be deemed of major significance to
  benefit the City. Naming or renaming a City asset for an individual is
  encouraged for those persons whose significance and good reputation have
  been accepted in the community or City; and/or state or national history; or
  iv. Major Donations. Financial contributions to the City may warrant
  acknowledging the funding source through naming or renaming. Such
  donations will require a donation agreement to address the use of the funds,
  length of naming recognition, and continued maintenance and operations
  costs.

  C. GUIDING PRINCIPLES
  1. General Provisions
  i. The City will also consider the following when considering nominations for
  naming or renaming of a City asset:
  a. Nominations that portray depictions, words, or phrases that the City
  reasonably deems to be harmful, controversial, or otherwise do not
  support the guiding principles stated in this policy will not be considered.
   b. Generally, an asset shall not be named after a public official or private
  individual unless that person is deceased. The naming of a City asset in
  honor of a deceased person shall generally not occur until after a
  minimum waiting period of one year.
  c. Generally, the naming of ancillary features or rooms may have names
  that differ from that of the entire property. These names shall be subject
  to the same criteria within this policy but may be more generously
  applied commensurate with the value of the named feature.
  d. If multiple donors share in the contribution, the City shall favor a
  functional title for the asset with plaques honoring those who
  contributed.
  e. If a civic group provides the contribution, only those whose mission
  statement is compatible with City goals and objectives shall be
  considered.
  f. No City asset shall be named after an elected official while that official
  remains in public office, and naming an asset after an elected official
  while in office will only be considered under extraordinary
  circumstances.
  g. Names shall not be subject to change unless the name has been in
  effect for 10 years or more and, after review the proposed new name is
  found to be more appropriate than the existing name based on the
  criteria in this policy.
  h. At any time, names shall be subject to change should the name become
  disreputable or does not otherwise support the guiding principles
  outlined in this policy.
  2. Corporate contributions shall be recognized within the framework of the
  City’s Advertising & Sponsorship Policy.
  3. All related signage shall comply with the applicable sections of the Palmdale
  Municipal Code.
  4. The City Council may authorize the feature of a park or open space to be
  developed or established through a fundraising effort that may include
  naming. This policy does not intend to prohibit fundraising activities that
  involve naming as part of the fundraising effort. Examples may include
  naming a brick, seats, and plants.

D. PROCEDURES
  1. Naming or Renaming Nomination Process
  i. Public input is accepted by submitting a City-provided application for
  naming or renaming a City asset. The City Manager or their designee will
  review nominations to evaluate alignment with the City’s naming policy.
  Reviewed nominations will be provided to the City Council in a written report
  to include project feasibility and cost estimates. Public nominations that are
  determined to be in alignment with this policy will require the
   Councilmember to endorse the nomination; the City Council may then hear
  endorsed nominations and consider approval.
  ii. Nominations initiated by individual Councilmembers shall be submitted to
  the City Council directly. Councilmembers may only initiate nominations for
  assets.
  iii. Nominations under the criteria of historical significance shall include an
  evaluation by a historian and/or a public Library director to validate facts.
  2. Naming or Renaming Approval Process
  i. Naming of City assets requires a majority vote of approval by the City
  Council.
  ii. Renaming of City assets requires a unanimous vote of approval by the City
  Council.
  iii. Generally, a facility shall not be named after an elected official or private
  individual unless that person is deceased. A decision to name a facility after
  an elected official who is not deceased shall require a unanimous vote of
  approval by the City Council.
  3. The City, in its sole discretion, may:
  i. Name rooms and property amenities to establish operational order or to
  coincide with a property theme. Street naming shall comply with current
  requirements and application procedures.
  ii. Provide a good faith, discretionary administration of this policy for the
  benefit of the public in general. This policy is not intended to provide an
  enforceable right, expectation, or property interest to any third party
  providing donations to the City.

E. DEFINITION OF TERMS
  “Amenities” shall mean an individual exterior or interior feature within a larger park
  or facility, including, but not limited to, meeting rooms, landscaped grounds, flower
  gardens, sculptures, picnic shelters, play lots, ball fields, and other similar items.

  “City Asset” shall include parks, facilities, streets, and amenities.

  “Donation” shall mean a monetary (cash) contribution, endowment, personal
  property, real property, financial securities, equipment, in-kind goods or services,
  or any other asset that the City has accepted and for which the donor has not
  received goods or services in return.

  “Donor” shall mean a person or other legal entity that proposes or provides a
  donation to the City.

  “Elected Official” shall mean any person who acquires local, regional, or national
  office through an election.
  “Funding” shall mean a financial or in-kind donation that may result in the naming
  or renaming of a City asset.

  “Historian” shall mean a scholar who studies and writes published historical
  narratives based on research and validation.
 “Naming” shall mean the selection and approval by the City Council for the initial
naming of a City asset.

“Renaming” shall mean the selection and approval by the City Council for a new
name of an existing City asset.

“Sign Ordinance” shall mean the City’s sign regulations contained in the
Palmdale Municipal Code.

BACKGROUND

On March 6, 2013, the City Council approved funding agreements with the Los Angeles
County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (LACMTA) for five projects along SR-14 and
Palmdale Blvd, authorizing the use of Measure R Equity Grant funds totaling $110 million.
Project No. 672, Palmdale Blvd (SR-138) and SR-14 Interchange Improvement Project is
the second Measure R project that will be going into construction to alleviate the existing
bottleneck configuration on the north and southbound SR-14 mainline and the storage
deficiency of the north and southbound off-ramps to Palmdale Boulevard.

This project will improve the circulation and operations of the interchange’s north and
southbound ramps and enhance safety and operations along Palmdale Boulevard with
improvements between 5th Street West, Division Street, and SR-138/SR-14. Due to the high
volume of traffic traveling along Palmdale Boulevard, motorists experience an extended
queue along the ramps, which backs onto the SR-14 mainline during heavy congestion
periods, creating a potential safety concern. To alleviate the traffic backup and improve the
safety of the interchange, a new northbound auxiliary lane and two southbound off-ramp
lanes will be constructed at Palmdale Boulevard. Additionally, the project includes a new
curb, gutter, sidewalks, ADA ramps, fencing, raised medians with irrigation and landscaping,
drainage improvements, streetlights, traffic signals, signing and striping, interchange
xeriscape landscaping, City Palmdale monument sign, and mural painting of the wall under
the Palmdale Boulevard under crossing.

In addition, due to the volume of work and size of the project, there is a need for an outside
project management firm to provide project management, the construction contract’s
administration, financial management, contract oversight services, and communications and
coordination with all the stakeholders.

considered by the Planning Commission and recommended for approval by the City
Council (General Plan Amendment 91-4, Pre-Zone 89-6, Specific Plan 89-3, and DA 92-
2; Resolution Nos. 92-13 and 91-114). The SP and EIR were subsequently approved by
the City Council (Resolution No. 92-58 and Ordinance No. 971) in March of 1992.

Development Agreement (DA) 92-2 became effective on May 8, 1993, with an expiration
date of May 10, 2013. On December 13, 2012, DA 92-2 was subsequently amended
(Development Agreement Amendment 12-01) to modify timing and mitigation fees
related to the construction of the required fire station. On March 6, 2013, the City Council

On March 14, 2005, the City Council approved Tentative Tract Map (TTM) 61894
through Resolution No. CC 2005-060, which established an expiration date of May 10,
2013. Subsequently, two legislative time extensions (Assembly Bill [AB] 333 and AB
208) were approved automatically, extending the map for a total of four years until May
10, 2017. On July 11, 2017, the City Council approved Resolution No. CC 2017-030 for
the first discretionary three-year time extension, which extended the expiration of the
map until May 10, 2020. Subsequently, on September 28, 2020, an 18-month time
extension pursuant to AB 1561 automatically extended the expiration of the map until
November 10, 2021. On November 17, 2020, the City Council approved a second and
final discretionary three-year time extension pursuant to Resolution No. CC 2020-102
extending the life of the map until November 10, 2024.

In 2021, the SP was amended (Specific Plan Amendment [SPA] 18-003) and renamed
to the Anaverde Nuevo Specific Plan (Ordinance No. 1573). The amendment increased
open space, reduced park space, reduced the overall number of dwelling units, allowed
for the development of active adult communities, reduced the size of future commercial
development, and eliminated the golf course. In conjunction with SPA 18-003, a Major
Modification to TTM 61894 was also approved (Resolution No. CC 2021-106), which
revised the conditions of approval to ensure consistency with the updated specific plan.
An Addendum to the 1992 EIR was adopted in conjunction with the SPA 18-003 and the
Major Modification to TTM 61894.

The currently approved conditions of approval for TTM 61894 include requirements
related to the construction of the bridge portion of Bridge Road. As currently conditioned,
two key milestones are identified:

    Plans for the bridge must be submitted and approved prior to the occupancy of the
  112th dwelling unit within TTM 61894 or the beginning of the construction of any
  other remaining portion of the SP.

    The bridge must be constructed and operational prior to the occupancy of the 223rd
  dwelling unit within TTM 61894 or the occupancy of any other unit within the
  remaining portion of the SP.

The Applicant is proposing to revise the conditions as follows:

  1) Allow design of the bridge to occur by the occupancy of the 448th dwelling unit and
  construction of the bridge to occur by the 518th dwelling unit.

  2) Reduce the required width of the bridge and roadway from 80/64 (total width/curb-
  to-curb width) to 70/54 and add a requirement for a minimum 4-foot-wide median.

  3) Eliminate specific requirements for the width of Bridge Road at certain
  intersections.

  4) Add a new condition of approval requiring the establishment of a Community
  Facilities District to help finance future infrastructure improvements and revisions
  to several conditions related to the width of Bridge Road have been proposed and
  are also outlined within the attached Resolution.

No revisions, other than those outlined within the attached Resolution, are proposed for
TTM 61894, and all other existing conditions of approval will remain applicable to the
project.

RECOMMENDATION

Council consideration to provide language interpretation services at all regular City
Council meetings.

BACKGROUND

At the February 21, 2024, meeting, the Council directed staff to conduct research on how
cities handle requests for language interpretation services at council meetings and bring
forth the information at a future council meeting.

DISCUSSION

The City offers language interpretation services at Council meetings on a by-request
basis, with a minimum of 72 hours advance notice.

Staff surveyed 29 cities and out of the 29 cities the following information was confirmed:

    59% require a 24, 48, or 72-hour request for interpretation services;
    24% have an outside interpreter at every meeting; and,
    17% have staff on standby to interpret as needed.

A detailed list of the cities surveyed is provided in the attached table.

The average cost for interpretation services, including equipment when needed, is
approximately $2,400 per meeting, with an average of 24 meetings per year. If directed
to move forward with providing services at each City Council meeting, the fiscal impact
would be $57,600 annually.
